speechtext:
That is a different proposition, but they should prove the fraud. It is an imposition to go back twenty-five or thirty years. If the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson) gets caught by their going back thirty years he will be the one who will do the kicking. I know the minister knows of many cases where they have gone back quite a ways.
If they go back that number of years the income tax branch will charge you interest on the amount computed. There should be a limitation of not more than five years on the time they can go back. No interest should be charged on the unpaid portions of succession duties. Many estates have been tied up for two or three years. I realize that the dominion government entered this field of taxation only a short time ago. As I say, the government should not charge interest on unpaid balances unless an account is first sent in to the trustee or the executor or whoever is in charge of the estate. This should apply also to income taxes. An account should first be presented before interest is charged.
The government said that the simplified tax forms which were issued last year could be filled out in ten minutes. Apparently the forms for those in the higher brackets are also extremely easy to decipher, because it appears that the income tax branch provides for the income tax officials a book on the income tax act which is printed in Montreal and priced at SI.25. They give all the officials in the income tax branch one of those books absolutely free so that they can work out what the government has set down. In other words, the government feels that the income tax officials in Ottawa and throughout the country cannot possibly work out the income tax problems unless they have this book costing $1.25. If they give these books to the officials, why should not the ordinary taxpayer be supplied with one? He certainly is the goat; he is the one who has to pay.

The Budget-Mr. Winkler
Last year I made a suggestion to the Minister of Finance. He took me up on it and he carried it out. He put in item 36 in the 1942 income tax form and it would appear that the Department of National Revenue did very well under that time. The following question appeared in a return under my name:
What is the total amount of money received to date under item 3G, general income tax T.l *form for the year 1942?
The minister's answer was:
The total amount of deferred tax received as of May 31, 1944, under item 36, T.l general 1942 is $4,743,111.
I should like again to make a suggestion to the minister which I made last year. The time for paying that deferred tax, the 1942 tax, for those who had an investment income, was April 30 of this year. That tax brought in 84,700.000. Would the minister not be wise to allow that to continue on in 1945 and 1946 or even longer? It is based on an expectancy of life table anyhow. If that went on, I know that many dollars would come in. We need the money now; we do not need it fifty years from now. I think the minister would be wise to accept my suggestion and allow that to carry on. I believe the minister would also be well advised to send out a notice to all those who are on that list telling them what their deferred tax is, and also send them a table of life expectancy such as I have here. I know very few people know that there is such a table got out by the government; in fact, many people do not know that there is such an item as item 36 in the tax form. They do not know that when they die the estate has to pay the balance of the tax. Many would like to pay it now. I would also suggest that instead of making people pay the whole tax at once, they be allowed to pay half or one-quarter or three-quarters or any portion they like, but at the same rate of discount as allowed before.	*
In regard to payroll deductions I have talked to industrial workers and many of them say, "We would rather that the government took 100 per cent of the tax instead of only 95 per cent, so that at the end of the year we would not have to pay the government five or ten or fifteen per cent, but would likely have the whole tax cleared off. If not, we should have to pay only a very small amount, and in some cases the government would owe us money and we would have money coming to us."
The budget imposes different rates of duty on different articles entering this country. There is one duty or luxury tax which I think should be removed entirely. I have mentioned this in the house before and I am mentioning it again now. I refer to the tax on the poor man's alarm clock. I think the tax should be taken off entirely on alarm clocks costing not more than $4.50. It is hard enough to get an alarm clock as it is, and the luxury tax should be taken off altogether.
I have a suggestion to make to the Minister of National Revenue. I have mentioned it before and am mentioning it again, and then I am through. In the city of Peterborough we have been asked to subscribe to the different victory loans. In the first loan our objective was $2,750,000 and we subscribed $3,085,000. In the second loan our objective was $2,750,000 and we subscribed $3,027,900. In the third loan our objective was $3,250,000 and we subscribed $3,546,450. In the fourth loan our objective was $4,350,000 and we subscribed $4,679,550. In the fifth loan our objective was $4,600,000 and we subscribed $4,700,000. In the sixth loan we went away over the top, subscribing over $4,700,000. The people of my district are doing everything possible to help the war effort, and I am going to ask the Minister of National Revenue, as I asked him last year, to open an income tax office in Peterborough, at least during the time when the returns are being filled out, and have there one or more men to help the taxpayers to make out their returns.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my main purpose in rising is to ask for consideration for infant industries in my riding of Lisgar in Manitoba. I know that is a very unusual request to make on the budget, but that is my main purpose in rising.
Before doing so I should like to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) especially upon removing entirely the duty on agricultural machinery. Prior to this budget the duty was only 7^ per cent, but that duty weighed heavily on the agricultural producer, especially in the west, because the implements of industry are so essential in production there, and with the mechanization of farms the cost is steadily rising, and therefore the task would have become increasingly burdensome. The removal of the duty has been something which has been sought ever since I can remember, and it is very gratifying indeed that it has actually come to pass at last.
I should also like to refer to the announcement which was made within recent weeks that United States funds would be forthcoming for those who wish to travel in the United States. I would suggest that the amount be extended so that those who require treatment for health, especially those with a delicate constitution, be permitted to visit the southern states in the winter time, particularly between

The Budget-Mr. Winkler

October and May, when the sun's rays become very oblique and when one becomes impoverished more or less from not receiving those rays on one's anatomy. Few of us are rugged Stefanssons, and very few of us regard the Arctic as friendly as Mr. Stefansson did. With the month of October or November arctic weather begins to encroach on the Dominion of Canada and one cannot very well receive the rays of the sun to advantage in this climate during the winter months. For that reason I believe it would be advantageous to the health of the Dominion of Canada if sufficient United States funds were forthcoming to permit people seeking health to visit the southern states. I do not anticipate that there would be any great difficulty in making the necessary arrangements. It would be an investment that would soon bring a return. Further, I do not think this country would lose a dollar by it because, as those of us who have ever travelled in the United States know, there are dozens of people wherever you go down there seeking information as to Canada's summer resorts and every Canadian who visited the southern states would be a missionary for our resorts. It would mean that twelve people from the United States for Canada's one would travel increasingly in Canada. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that this country would not lose one dollar.
Speaking of tourists, when this war ends, as we all hope it will soon, and it may end suddenly, the United States tourist, who is a great traveller by car, will possibly try to enter the Dominion of Canada. The constituency of Lisgar, which I have the honour to represent, extends along the international boundary line for seventy-eight miles. There is no barrier, no river whatever, nothing to prevent anyone from crossing the border. Five United States macadam roads approach the boundaries of my constituency. Two of them meet Canadian roads; the other three do not. I assume that this situation could be described as fairly general in the Dominion of Canada, where we are not too amply equipped to meet the tourist demands which will likely follow the war. I therefore suggest that consideration be given to the creation of a fund which would permit the provinces, already impoverished as we know, to enter upon the construction of all-weather roads which lead to the United States.
There are two industries to which I wish particularly to refer. The first, which is only two years old is known as the bentonite industry. There is in Canada only one deposit of this material which is being worked. As the age of the industry would indicate, it is a war-

time enterprise, and made possible only by the war. I emphasize the words "made possible." As many know, this metal is a volcanic ash which was deposited on portions of this country in prehistoric days, or rather, deposited on the ancient sea and washed into coves and deposited in beds ranging from a few inches to several feet deep. That clay or rock is mined very readily. Inasmuch as at one time it was subjected to intense heat it is suitable for certain purposes connected with war-time industry. It acts, among other ways, as a filter which is necessary in the production of oil and gasoline. It also acts r. s a catalyst in the production of synthetic rubber. Its most useful purpose before the advent of the oil business was as a binder for moulding sands in steel foundries. These are the three purposes for which it is needed, and one can readily surmise that war industries cannot get along without it.
There is one corporation in the United States with which this company is now competing. The Manitoba company is a joint stock company organized among farmers, although there are a few lawyers and quite a number of artisans interested in it. One might call it a shoe-string company; it used a lot of makeshift machinery since the promoters did not know what they would be up against, but they now have a pretty good plant, because of the expansion made possible by the war. The United States firm could easily run them out of business, but for one thing: at the present time it has about all it can look after in filling United States orders and practically none of its product is coming to Canada. Under these circumstances one would think that ordinarily the Canadian industry would have a fairly good chance to survive, but here is what it is up against. The company is not asking for tariff protection to exclude the United States competitor after the war, but it would like to be treated at least with fairness with regard especially to freight rates.
I wish to place a few figures before the house regarding freight rates on the raw clay from Jackson, Mississippi, to Sarnia, as compared with the rate for the same commodity from Winnipeg to Sarnia. In Canadian dollars the rate from Jackson is $7.40 per ton, as against $8.50 per ton by the Canadian National Railways from Winnipeg. Of course the distance from Jackson is shorter than that from Winnipeg, being 995 miles as against 1,500 by the Canadian National; however, a direct line from Winnipeg to Sarnia would lead through the United States, this route having a mileage of 1,113. There is not any great complaint about the difference as regards freight

The Budget-Mr. Winkler
on raw clay, but the activated clay, that is clay which has been treated and rendered suitable for the purpose for which it is intended, is a different matter. The freight in Canadian funds from Jackson, Mississippi, is only $9.46 per ton as against the Canadian rate of $16.00 per ton. This indicates far too wide a differential, $8.10 per ton on Canadian shipments as compared with $2.06 in respect of United States shipments. If that disparity is permitted to continue after the war, the Canadian company cannot begin to compete with the United States vrcpariy, and, it is safe to say, would be forced out of business. What would be lost? First, the company, which now employs a good many people-I do not know the exact number-would cease to exist. Last year it paid in freight rates to the Canadian National Railways over sixty thousand dollars. The other loss would be that of post-war expansion, the hope of enlarging the plant and thereby giving employment to ex-servicemen when they return.
There is another handicap under which the company operates and for which it has sought redress, but without result so far. It has asked for the milling-in-transit rate. Those hon. members who are accustomed to concerning themselves with the wheat milling business know that Canadian mills are accorded a milling-in-transit rate, which is a nominal rate with a stopover privilege; that is, the grain is brought a considerable distance in the bulk state, and is dumped into mills or elevators, at Kenora, at Winnipeg, at the head of the lakes and farther east too. This stopover privilege means quite a bit to the millers; they can, as I said, ship and mill products with a nominal charge for the stopover privilege. The bentonite company, which is known as Pembina Clays Limited, has been refused this privilege; and I think the time has come when this matter should be made public, because it is apparent that this young company, energetic and virile as it is, cannot hope to survive post-war competitive conditions unless it has some redress for the handicaps which I have described.
There is in my constituency another industry which is also in the infant stage; it is that of corn growing. It also was pioneered, as far as western Canada is concerned, in the constituency of Lisgar, and in the eastern half of that constituency practically all the grain corn in western Canada is grown. In 1941, when we had a very good crop, about twenty per cent of Canada's production was raised in that small area. Since then we have run into difficulty. In 1942 we had eight killing frosts in September, night after night,
and the crop was virtually ruined. In 1943 there was a considerable improvement, but still there was very cold weather all through the season and cold weather is not at all suitable for corn growing. In that district we have twelve commercial corn driers, and it could safely be described as a thriving industry up to a point. In my own case, com on the farm with which I am connected is used as a substitute for summer-fallow, but in most cases it is used as a cash crop by the small-acreage farmers.
In 1941 freight assistance was started in connection with the bringing of grains to eastern Canada. It was first announced that corn would be included in those grains, but later that was withdrawn and still later it was mentioned that, instead of western corn coming to Montreal, which is the main market, it would be accorded a freight subsidy from Calgary and Edmonton to Vancouver, instead of from the head of the lakes to Montreal. Under that arrangement in 1941, from October to December, 17,420 bushels were shipped to Vancouver; in 1942 a portion of the crop, 162,200 bushels, and in 1943 only 80,679 bushels, which would indicate that less than ten per cent of the product from our district has been shipped to Vancouver. All the rest, I am told by those who engage in the drying, shipping and selling, has been disposed of, mainly in Saskatchewan and some in Alberta.
It has come to my notice around the corridors of this building, I have been told by several persons, that the Ontario farmer does not like to see Manitoba corn sold in Ontario. I think that is a mistaken idea, because there is as much difference between Ontario and Manitoba corn as there is between Ontario and Manitoba wheat. The wheat of Ontario produces the best pastry flour; our wheat, of course, is, as we think, better for producing bread flour. The same holds in regard to corn. Eastern corn is starchy and produces corn starch and corn syrup, which the western com cannot under any circumstances as yet produce. Western corn is highly protein and produces the best chick feed and corn meal. In 1941 western corn was sold in Ontario at twelve cents a bushel over Ontario corn, the reason being that the demand for corn meal and chick feed was such as to force the price up. This did not mean that the situation would always be so, but that was the condition then. I think that explains roughly why our western corn is sometimes in demand over eastern corn, although at times during the last two years eastern wheat has been at a premium over western wheat.
What we would like to see is a fund set aside so that a freight subsidy on com will be
The Budget-Mr. Winkler

returned to the Fort William-Montreal point after the British Columbia market has been satisfied. We have run into this difficulty, that the companies of British Columbia, which are in the habit of dealing in corn, do not particularly like our Manitoba corn. They are accustomed to Argentine and South African corn, and a good many dealers in Manitoba who have been shipping say that they will ship no more corn there. If we should again have as large a crop as in 1941 we would be under a considerable handicap in having to ship it to Montreal in competition with other grains which receive a freight subsidy.
In that connection I would refer to sessional paper 345 dated June 2, 1944, moved for by the hon. member for Colchester-Hants (Mr. Purdy). What I am endeavouring to show is that in asking for this freight subsidy the people of Manitoba are not asking for anything unreasonable because, when one looks over the freight subsidies over the years, it would indicate that Manitoba has not been at all grasping in what she has obtained. This order asks for costs of federal assistance for twenty years. I have in my hand only the part that refers to the Department of Agriculture which covers the years from 1936 to the present time. In that period $53,937,000 was paid by the dominion government in freight subsidies. The province that received the most was Ontario, with $15,357,000-1 will not give the odd dollars. Saskatchewan and Quebec almost tied for second place. The second last was Prince Edward Island, with $944,000, and last of all was Manitoba with $352,000. The total, as I said, was $53,937,000. So that in asking for the return of the freight subsidy on corn from Fort William to Montreal we of southern Manitoba are not asking anything unreasonable.
There is in my riding another industry, not yet born, which I would refer to in passing. It is to be known as the vegetable oil extraction industry to be located at the village of Altona, where 16,000 acres of sunflowers are being grown by cooperative producers in that vicinity. In addition to the 16,000 acres there are a great many more on nearby farms not under arrangement with the cooperatives, although it can safely be said that com and the sunflower industry go hand in hand. It appears that, inasmuch as the cooperatives diesire themselves to go into the oil extraction business, there has been considerable feeling on the part of private industry that this is a mistake and should not be permitted or encouraged. On the other hand, I think that attitude is a mistake, because I am a firm believer in the idea that cooperatives and

private industry can exist side by side. I do not wish to go into details with regard to the attempts to establish this industry, but I mention it in passing and will refer to it when it comes up under another item.
I should like to say before taking my seat that I have been a member of one or more cooperatives since 1915, and at the present time I am a member of two. I also take an equal or a greater interest in private industry, because I am connected with agriculture and I have great faith that agriculture will remain a private industry inasmuch as we are individualists. I think that is all I need say at this time.

Mr. Speaker, the budget speech has made it clear that our war expenditures, far from being decreased, as we had been given to understand in previous discussions, will be increased to such an extent that they will reach the tremendous figure of $5,300.000,000, which will bring our total expenditures to $6,000,000,000 for 1944-45. In view of the statement which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made in this house on March 30, 1939, when he said that our country did not have unlimited powers and referred to the heavy burden of our national debt which then amounted only to $3,385,000,000, while to-day it reaches the sum of about $11,000,000,000 and will be $14,000,000,000 at the end of the fiscal year, Canadians have every reason to entertain fears about the future of their country.
I for one do not hesitate to repeat that our war effort is beyond our means, that it is leading us to ruin, and that it is a breach of the pledges that were given to the people. To meet those expenditures, the government is resorting to taxes, especially the income tax, and to loans.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) complained the other day about those who sell their victory bonds. That is unavoidable for the very reason that the country has exceeded its financial capacity-

As I was saying a moment ago, I wished to set out the guiding principles quoted in support of the claim that the CBC was an independent and self-governing body, free from governmental interference. I regret to say that the facts are not in accordance with these contentions. I call the attention of the house to the 1942 plebiscite. As soon as the plebiscite was announced, the League for the Defence of Canada was organized in Montreal. On February 13, 1942, the secretary of the League wrote to Mr. Augustin Frigon, assistant general manager of the CBC, requesting the use of the CBC radio stations. On February 16, 1942, Mr. Frigon replied as follows:
Most likely, our regulations, Which apply to general elections, will be enforced during the campaign which, in all probability, will precede the plebiscite announced by the government of Canada.
Our services are offered free of charge to all recognized political parties, and according to a policy which was adopted almost three years ago. I feel that so far we have observed, in this regard, a strict neutrality.
To sum up, your league may use individual private stations, but our corporation, in view of its national character, must remain neutral in any political matters.
The secretary of the League for the Defence of Canada replied that it was not a case of conducting elections or electoral campaigns or ascertaining the views of the parties or electing a party in preference to another, and that the policy mentioned in Mr. Frigon's letter should not apply in this case.
On February 24, Mr. Frigon wrote as follows to the secretary of the League for the Defence of Canada:
Our regulations in regard to the broadcasting over the CBC stations and networks of political

The Budget-Mr. Raymond
or controversial matters are quite clear and do not allow any other interpretation than that given in my letter of February 16.
I shall deem it a duty to convey to the proper authorities the remarks contained in your letter of February 18. In view of the importance of the plebiscite and the peculiar conditions of the campaign which will be waged on this issue, it is quite possible that our board of governors will place a special interpretation on our regulations.
And on February 28, 1942, Messrs. Murray and Frigon communicated the following message by telephone:
(Text):
The broadcasting arrangements for the publicity are still under consideration, and the league's claims are being taken fully into account; decision cannot be taken until the enabling bill becomes law. Meanwhile the league for the defence of Canada is in the same position as any other political organization.
(Translation): The act ordering the plebiscite was passed on March 5, and there was another exchange of correspondence. On March 11, Mr. Frigon wrote to the secretary of the league, as follows:
Nothing has been decided yet about the use of the stations and networks of our corporation for the discussion of the problem connected with the plebiscite recently ordered by parliament. So far, your request is the only one which we have received for the use of our stations.
On March 30, the secretary of the league wrote to Mr. Frigon, as follows:
The newspapers announce that the Prime Minister will soon speak on the question.
Should we understand that you have come to a decision, and would you be kind enough to let us know what that decision is.
There was no answer to that letter. But on April 4, the press announced that the Right Hon. Mr. King, Hon. Mr. Hanson, Mr. Blaclcmore and others would broadcast on the question. The league wrote another letter, and finally on April 8, the secretary received the following answer:
Ottawa, April 8, 1942. Mr. Andre Laurendeau,
League for1 the defence of Canada.
Dear Sir,
In accordance with instructions received from the federal government, our corporation has placed at the disposal of the administration a certain number of periods on its various networks for the use of speakers who will discuss the plebiscite.
Your last letter, dated April 4, shows that you already know' how the transcontinental network is to be used in that connection. Eight half-hour periods will also be allotted to this matter on our French network. We have not yet been informed of the names of the speakers.
Such is the position. It is claimed that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is absolutely independent of any governmental control, but we have a convincing proof of
the contrary, in the letter from Mr. Frigon, assistant general manager, who states:
In accordance with instructions received from the federal government, our corporation has placed at the disposal of the administration a certain number of periods on its various networks for the use of speakers who will discuss the plebiscite.
You call it an independent corporation. Yes, to camouflage all the government's propaganda over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's stations.
. We had been asked to answer "Yes" or "No", but all those who were in favour of an affirmative answer had the opportunity of speaking over the radio, including the leader of the social credit, Mr. Hanson and Mr. Coldwell.
But all those who were in favour of a "No" vote were prevented from using the facilities of the national network. Even our offer to pay for the use of the radio, was turned down. Let us stop fooling the public by leading them to believe that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is independent while it is a political tool of the government. We hear much talk of freedom, justice and democracy. It would be better to respect those principles in Canada before attempting to enforce them somewhere else.
The 30 per cent of our people who voted "No" and who contribute to the maintenance of the corporation had the same rights as the other 70 per cent who voted "Yes", if it be true that the corporation's object is to ensure the expression of opinions, and that its guiding principles, that I just quoted, are that the radio waves belong to the public and that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has among its objects that of ensuring that the various views on matters relating to questions of foremost importance will be expounded.
Here is a matter of foremost importance, yet the proponents of the negative vote were barred from expressing their views through the facilities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I wish to quote the following excerpt from an article published in Saturday Night by Mr. Sandwell, who is at present, I believe, one of the governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I quote:
(Text):
The Freneh-Canadian press is regarding with a sort of cynical amusement the attacks which are being directed against the CBC in connection with the Bracken broadcast and-though these are dying down-the "Things to Come" series. For the Freneh-Canadian press has a long memory, and it is now recalling, with ample justification, the fact that from no Englishspeaking source did there come any protest against the extraordinary error of policy by
The Budget-Mr. Raymond

which the CBC refused to allow any broadcasting from its stations on the No side of the plebiscite campaign. It is difficult at this distance of time to understand, and quite impossible to justify, that profoundly illogical policy. The people having been asked by their government to express their views upon a specific question, the arguments upon both sides of that question should have been presented with equal freedom. It was not treasonable, it was not even contrary to the defence of Canada regulations, to vote or to argue on the No side. The press was permitted to disseminate No arguments; the private radio stations had equal freedom. But the CBC carried the Yes arguments and the Yes arguments alone. The policy was not only illogical, it was most unwise. Its result in Freneh-Canada was to increase the No vote by creating the impression that the Yes case was being stuffed down the throats of the Frencli Canadians.
We have to express our own penitence for not having raised our voice against this piece of unwisdom at the time. Our only excuse is that we entirely failed to realize its import.
(Translation):	I am very glad that Mr. Sandwell has been appointed one of the governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I hope that such mistakes will not recur.
Here is another instance. Two or three days after Doctor Gauthier had been appointed organizer for the Bloc Populaire in the Quebec district, he was arrested and it was announced all over the country, through the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, that Doctor Gauthier, organizer for the Bloc Populaire in the Quebec district, had been arrested and court-martialed. There was no ground for the charge laid in that case, as was shown by the evidence; that fact was known and an attempt was made to bring him into disrepute only because he had just been appointed organizer for the Bloc Populaire. For many weeks that trial was mentioned over the radio, and each time it was stated that Doctor Gauthier was an organizer for the Bloc Populaire. When he was acquitted after the court which tried the case had deliberated for a few minutes only, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation merely announced that Doctor Gauthier had been acquitted. For once, the words "organizer for the Bloc Populaire" were omitted, and some people would afterwards have the public believe that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is not a political organization, that it is a body free from political influence and government interference.
I wanted the public to be aware of these facts. If the complaint is sometimes voiced that we lack confidence in our public men, all I can say is that they well deserve what they get since they have been deluding the people far too long.
One more remark before I conclude. In. the course of the debate this afternoon, the Min-

ister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) intimated that farmers' sons were no longer called up for military service. I regret to say that I know of cases where such men are still summoned for military duty. I regret to say that some farmers' sons asked for postponement months ago that they might work on the farm, and they have received no reply or have been turned down. I also regret that the inquiry requested by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) concerning happenings in British Columbia where force has been used to have recruits signed up for active service has not been granted. I have received many letters dealing with this matter and a recent message was really heart-rending. It concerned a sick recruit who called on the doctor for treatment. The first question which the doctor asked him was; "Have you signed up for active duty?" As the recruit replied "no," the doctor refused to look after him. These are the means resorted to in order to compel men to enlist for active service. And yet the public is still led to believe that we are following the voluntary system! Well, if we wisn to retain the confidence of the public let us cease to mislead them.

^ Mr. P. E. WRIGHT (Melfort): Mr. Speaker in taking part in this budget debate I intend to restrict my remarks to one particular section of the speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), namely, that dealing with trade and tariff policies.
I think we are all agreed that the freer movement of trade in the after-war years is essential not only to our own prosperity but for the peace and welfare of the world as a whole, and any movement made to bring about that desirable end is welcome at this time. I should like, however, to point out to the minister the position of the various countries of the world. They have changed to a remarkable degree during the past five years, and if we are to export our goods to them we must be prepared to take in exchange for our goods either manufactured goods or raw materials from the rest of the world. Every nation both large and small has increased its manufacturing capacity during the war years, and every other nation will be doing just what Canada is doing after the war, seeking to find a market for exportable surpluses. This can mean only one thing, that we must be prepared to take other goods in exchange for our own.
It appears to me that the problem of prosperity after the war is not entirely one of finding export markets but rather one of every nation being able to increase its own capacity

The Budget-Mr. Wright
to use goods and services. In other words, each individual nation has to organize its internal economy so as to raise the purchasing power and standard of living of its own people, so that we may all be able to use more goods than we were able to consume in the nineteen-thirties. The freer exchange and export of goods has its place but, as I listen to government members and read certain papers in this country, it seems to me that in placing responsibility for a prosperous Canada on export trade alone they are on very narrow ground indeed. As a matter of fact, I think it is just looking for an excuse to go back to the conditions which existed before the war. During the depression years that was the story to which we listened, that we could have prosperity only if other nations were prepared to buy from us larger quantities of goods and services than we were prepared to buy from them. For five years under the Tory government of Mr. Bennett we starved at home in order that we might have a favourable balance of trade and in order that we might export more than we imported. We in this group believe that if we are to have this freer movement of trade which everyone desires we cannot leave it to the exporters and importers. We believe that we must have government export and import boards that will be prepared to give direction and, if necessary, assistance in these exports.
In the past we have only exported when the exporter could make a profit, and to make that profit the exporter very often found that he had to force the price of the article which he was exporting on the domestic market down low enough to make a profit on it when he wanted to export it. Therefore we found that a small exportable surplus of five or ten per cent of any particular article controlled our domestic price. Take beef and butter, for example, before the war, and eggs as another example. Before the war we found that in the summer months in western Canada eggs could be bought at seven cents a dozen, while five months later in November and December the same eggs were worth fifty cents a dozen. No industry can be prosperous with price fluctuations such as that, and the price fluctuations are caused largely by the fact that when surpluses come on the market they have to be exported and the exporter has to force the price down to where he can make a profit on it. On the other hand, we have found that certain companies which had a monopoly and complete control over the price structure of the article which they had to sell have often used our domestic market as a means ofbonus-ing their export trade. We have found this in our cereals I have seen advertisements, for
instance, for breakfast foods made in western Canada in the city of Saskatoon offered for less money in London than had to be paid for them right opposite the factory at home. These conditions have not led in the past to freer trade but rather to restrictions and world cartels and monopolies which have divided the world into economic spheres of influence, which has been one of the major factors in causing world wars in the past.
We believe that the duty of these government export and import boards would be to see to it that we have a freer movement of goods both out of and into Canada. These boards would be used as an instrument of government policy in creating better and larger markets for Canada's exports and1 controlling our imports so as to fit them into an expanding Canadian economy.
We do not believe, however, as the government does that we should use the fact that other nations are not prepared to go as far as we are as an excuse for doing nothing at home. Our domestic market is our largest market. Up to the outbreak of the war approximately seventy-five per cent of all the goods and services produced in Canada were used here. This is something over which we have complete control, and we cannot say that we have done our best as long as there is one home in Canada that lacks anything which can be produced in this country. This leaves a wide field open, and neither this nor any other government has the right to use the hackneyed excuse that lack of world trade prevents us from having prosperity. It is, after all, only surpluses that we need for export.
In this pre-election budget the Minister of Finance keeps a promise that was given by the Liberals some twenty-five years ago when he removes the tariff on farm implements. In other words, he gave to the implement manufacturing companies twenty-five years notice of the government's intention, and then the government seems to be surprised that these companies have so arranged their business largely to nullify, so far as the farmer is concerned, the beneficial effects of this lower tariff. The minister himself states at page 4183 of Hansard of June 26, 1944:
Changes in the custom tariff would here and now have little, if any, effect on the supply or cost of goods.
That was the government's experience in the past when they reduced the tariff on farm implements. In 1935 the government reduced the tariff on these products from. 25 per cent to 124 per cent, and the price of farm implements promptly went up 4-4 per cent. As a result a committee was set up in Ottawa to in-
451S
The Budget-Mr. Wright.

vestigate the prices of farm, implements. That committee brought in certain findings. But have the government done anything about those findings? I am going to read a few as they appear in the minutes and proceedings, report No. 20, on farm implement prices by the special committee appointed by the House of Commons in 1937. I will not read all these recommendations, since there are thirty-six of them, but will read just a few to show what the government have failed to do in carrying out the committee's proposals:
7. That farmers have a right to expect the level of farm implements to be based on the most efficient and economical manufacturing and distribution cost. . . .
13. That the matter of freight rates on farm implements should receive immediate attention with a view to restoring lower rates thereon.
There has been no change in freight rates on farm implements since that time.
22. That indirectly this retention of profits in the United States affected the price level of farm implements in Canada, as tile true profits arising out of their Canadian operations were not properly appreciated by the United States companies.
I shall have more to say about that later on.
24. That the companies should encourage the further standardization of replacement parts in the same implements manufactured by different companies and in addition standardization of the implements themselves.
Well, the government has done nothing during the past number of years to see that these recommendations in regard to standardization are carried out.
28.	That the profits to the farm implement companies on the sale of replacement parts is excessive, and the price of these to the consumer should be materially reduced.
They have been going up steadily ever since.
29.	That the increases announced by the companies in January, 1936, were not justified by an increase in manufacturing or distribution costs or by the financial results of the companies in so far as these were affected by the price level of farm implements.
Yet nothing has been done about it.
30.	That over the period 1891 to 1936 retail prices of farm implements have been maintained at too high a level as shown by the financial returns to the companies engaged in the industry, during that period. . . .
33. That the committee is of the opinion that the cost of distribution of farm implements is unnecessarily high and constitutes an important factor in the prices to the consumers.
These are recommendations made by the Ottawa committee. As a result of the failure of this government to carry out any- of these recommendations, in 1939 a Liberal government in Saskatchewan set up another com-

mittee to investigate this matter. On page 10 of sessional paper No. 124 of the Saskatchewan legislature it has this to say with respect to this matter. The findings and recommendations of the select special committee on farm implement prices and distribution include the following:
Early in 1936, the companies announced an increase of price in farm implements amounting to 4-4 per cent as found by the Ottawa committee. It w'as this particular increase, announced after a substantial reduction in the tariff from 25 per cent to 12J per cent, that gave rise to the Ottawa inquiry. Despite a further reduction in the tariff to 7J per cent and despite the findings of the Ottawa committee that this increase was not justified and that the prices of farm implements had been, over the years 1913-1936, too high, despite, too, a definite finding that there was an excessive mark-up over cost on cream separators and repair parts, and that the prices of these should be particularly and substantially reduced, this committee finds that none of these findings wrere given effect to, and that, in addition, further price increases occurred in 1937.
As this report states, the dominion government set up in 1937 a special committee to investigate this matter, and despite the fact that they spent thousands of dollars in this investigation and made the findings some of which I have read into the record to-night, they failed to follow up the investigation by taking any concrete action to give effect to those findings. As a matter of fact, the only people who made anything out of those proceedings were the counsel hired by the government, and they were paid a nice fat fee for their services on the various commissions. It was as a result of this that in 1939 a Liberal government set up another committee. They, too, brought in certain recommendations, but -again-the government failed to take any action with respect to them. I am going to read some of the things which the Saskatchewan investigation committee recommended. It states, on page 27 of its report:
This committee is of the opinion that, in the light of the findings in these two reports-
That is, the Ottawa report and the Saskatchewan report.
-and because of the general knowledge of the maintenance of prices at a given level by all companies engaged in the industry, a fair inference can be drawn that a tacit agreement exists between the companies to maintain substantially uniform prices above the level justified by manufacturing and distribution costs plus a reasonable profit.
This committee made a recommendation which, as stated on page 47 of the report, is as follows:
That, as the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act of the dominion appear to

The Budget-Mr. Wright
have been violated by the major companies in the industry, consideration should be given to instituting proceedings under the said act.
I ask this government if they have taken any action with regard to this monopoly control of the price of farm implements. Did the Saskatchewan government take any action with regard to it? None whatever. One of the reasons for the defeat of the Saskatchewan government in the last election was that they had taken no concrete action with respect to the findings of this committee. I say further that one of the reasons for the defeat of the present government when they go to the polls this fall will be the fact that they have failed to take any concrete action with regard to the findings of this committee and other committees which have been set up by this government. It reminds me of a story which an old gentleman who was the chairman of one of my recent meetings in the west told me. He said that the present old political parties reminded him very much of a flock of old hens which he kept over one year; he said they" did an awful lot of cackling for all the eggs they laid. That has been the position of the present government; they have done a lot of cackling for all the concrete action which they have put into effect to remedy some of these things.

further to say about that later on, as to who will control that company. In the report of the committee appointed in the United States in 1935 to investigate the farm machine industry the following appears:
The effect on prices of this concentration of production is such that, with respect to the most important farm implements, the prices established by the leading manufacturers, especially International Harvester Company and Deere and Company, constitute in so far as the machines are of a closely similar character, the price level which all manufacturers observe.

The Ottawa committee, appointed by this government, state:
The committee is of the opinion, as a result of the above finding, that there is competition in the matter of securing sales but little or no effective competition in the matter of prices as between companies. . . . The companies state that it is the practice in the industry to exchange price lists and it may well be that this practice enables the companies to quickly gain uniformity in the matter of price levels.
Now you have the opinion of every committee that has been appointed, and I think it is quite evident from these findings that if this government is genuine in its desire to assist the farmers it will have to go much further and take further action than simply the removal of tariffs from farm implements. I would ask the minister if it is the intention of the government to remove the dumping duty on the importation of farm implements and parts? That is to say, if farmers or a cooperative wish to go over to the United States and go bargain hunting for cheaper implements, should they secure such implements will they be allowed to import them without duty, or will the dumping duty be placed on them and the retail price in the United States paid? This is a very important matter if we are to get any benefit from the
The Budget-Mr. Wright

reduction in tariff, and I believe it is something which the minister will have to take into consideration.
I am strongly of the opinion that if the government is genuine in its desire to help the farming industry one of the best ways in which it can do so is by assisting the cooperatives in western Canada in entering the farm machine industry. That was the finding of the Saskatchewan committee, and it was one of the recommendations of the Ottawa committee. As indicated in the Saskatchewan report at page 29, the committee-
. . . recommends the development in this province of a cooperative movement among the farmers to handle and distribute farm implements with a view to substantially reducing the cost. The committee feels that the farmers of this province, individually, and collectively in such cooperative groups, should have every source of supply opened up to them if their efforts to reduce prices are to be successful.
One of the ways in which this government might assist in this matter is by seeing, when the war is over, that government plant and equipment which might be suitable for the manufacturing of farm implements should be turned over to the cooperatives already formed in western Canada for the purpose of manufacturing and distributing implements at reasonable prices, and every assistance should be given them in supplying their needs.
In 1939, as a result of the Saskatchewan investigation, Canadian Cooperative Implements Limited, a cooperative company, was set up with head offices in Regina, to take definite action with respect to the manufacture and distribution of farm implements. It was incorporated under dominion act with an authorized capitalization of SI million, and a large portion of this capitalization has already been collected in cash from the farmers supporting this cooperative in the west. The cooperative, however, have been unable to obtain the allotment of farm machinery because they were not in operation prior to the setting up of the wartime prices and trade board. They are at the present time affiliated with United States cooperatives and have bought a manufacturing plant in the United States which is now engaged in manufacturing war supplies but which, immediately on the conclusion of the war, will be used for the manufacture of tractors for distribution cooperatively in both the United States and Canada. It is only reasonable to expect that this government should first give to this cooperative a quota of farm implements and repair parts. That is something the government should see to immediately, as soon as implements are available.

speechtext: That has already been taken care of.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, they are certainly not able to distribute farm machinery as yet; the only thing they handle is second-hand machinery.

speechtext: The correspondence in the matter has got to the point where understandings are being reached.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad to hear that and I hope that something definite is done about it. It is over two years since the company was set up.
In the second place the government should see to it that, after the war, plant and equipment are made available to the cooperative for manufacturing any particular line of cooperative farm implements in the dominion that they wish. As shown in these reports, to all intents and purposes a monopoly in this industry exists in Canada and the United States, and this monopoly has flouted the government in the matter of reducing prices when tariffs were reduced. In fact, the Saskatchewan committee, at page 35 of their report, state:
This committee is of the opinion that, where a reduction in duty does not result in a reduction in price, it is because of a tacit agreement between the leaders in .industry that the savings resulting from the tariff [DOT] reductions will not be reflected in a lower price and the resultant maintenance of the .former and unjustified price level. The committee is further of the opinion that, where the effect of such reductions in duty is ignored by the companies concerned, this should be constantly and persistently brought to the attention of the consuming public. If this is done, the committee believes that it will have a salutary effect on the companies and that, as a result, the companies engaged in the industry will be forced to pass the savings on to the consumer.
What a pious hope, that one of these monopolies in the United States will be affected by public opinion in Canada when our own government has not backbone enough to institute proceedings against them under an act which the government itself has drawn up and which it admits that it believes the companies are flouting!

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I must say that this public opinion has never had the desired effect in the past, and I would strongly urge that the government take definite steps at this time to see that the 7i per cent tariff reduction is passed on to the farmer, together with the ten per cent reduction in the war exchange tax. The only reason given by the companies

The Budget-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford)
for not passing on these benefits to the consumers was that they were losing money on their Canadian companies. This fact, however, was not borne out by evidence submitted both to the committee in Ottawa and to the committee in Regina. The Ottawa committee found that the International Harvester company, Deere and Company, and other companies in a similar position when importing from the United States to serve the Canadian market, retained substantial profits arising out of the Canadian business, and that in examining the Canadian results no consideration was given to this amount retained in the United States being properly attributable to the Canadian business. To illustrate, in the period 1926 to 1935 inclusive, which it will be noted included five quite abnormal depression years, the International Harvester Company showed in its Canadian books a profit of $7,500,000 before payment of income tax. However, it was found that an additional $17,000,000 of profits had been retained in the United States, making the total profits accruing from the Canadian business some $24,000,000. In excuse the company stated that they were of the opinion that unless they invoiced all their goods to the Canadian company at a fair market value as determined by the Department of National Revenue, a dumping duty would be imposed. That is why I say it is very important that this government do something about the dumping duty.
In view of all these investigations and the findings which have been brought down I would strongly urge upon the government the desirability of either establishing a government-owned plant for the manufacture of farm implements in Canada immediately after the war, or giving the necessary assistance to enable the cooperatives of western Canada to establish a plant of their own in order to break this monopoly which, without doubt, exists in the farm implement industry in Canada.
This government has paid a great deal of lip-service to cooperatives. I should like to see it lay a few eggs that would be of some benefit to the cooperative industry. The Canadian federation of agriculture and various other agricultural bodies throughout Canada have been urging the necessity of a cooperative act in Canada. I should like to read from a booklet entitled, "Post-War Reconstruction for Agriculture", issued by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, in which they say:
Canada would be well advised to go all-out in encouraging people's cooperatives as a positive feature of reconstruction policy.
A federal cooperative act, to clearly define the principles, the rights and the place of cooperatives in our national economy is needed at once.
While paying this lip-service the government has failed to clarify the position of the cooperatives in Canada, with respect to taxation. Therefore I say that two things which should be done immediately are these. The government should give assistance to the cooperatives in western Canada which have been formed for the purpose of manufacturing and distributing machinery, and should bring in at this session a cooperative act which will clarify the position of the cooperatives with regard to taxation in Canada.
On motion of Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) the debate was adjourned.
